quiz.title: How well do you know Athanasios Diakos?
quiz.intro: Three quick questions from the film and its article.

questions.q: Where did Athanasios Diakos make his stand in April 1821?
options: At the bridge of Alamana, near Thermopylae
questions.explain: Diakos held the bridge at Alamana, about two kilometres from the pass at Thermopylae, in one of the first major battles of the War of Independence.

questions.q: After his capture, what did the Ottoman commander Omer Vrioni offer him?
options: His life, if he converted to Islam
questions.explain: He was offered his life if he converted to Islam and served the Ottomans. He refused, and he was executed days after the battle.

questions.q: What does the name Athanasios mean?
questions.explain: Athanasios comes from athanatos: not dying, immortal.

qa.title: Who was Athanasios Diakos?
answer: Athanasios Diakos was a Greek commander of the War of Independence. He had trained as a deacon, which is where the name Diakos comes from, before becoming a klepht, one of the mountain fighters who resisted Ottoman rule.

In April 1821 he held the bridge of Alamana, near Thermopylae, against a much larger Ottoman force. Captured after the battle, he was offered his life if he converted to Islam. He refused and was executed. A monument to him stands at Thermopylae, near the monument to Leonidas.

quiz.title: How well do you know the story of the hidden faith?
quiz.intro: Three quick questions from the film and its article.

questions.explain: The Vallahades were Greek-speaking Muslims of western Macedonia who kept much of their Greek language and culture for generations after converting.

questions.q: Where does the name Vallahades come from?
questions.explain: The name comes from the oath wa-llahi, which they used in everyday speech.

questions.q: In the 1923 population exchange, how were the Vallahades classified?
options: By their religion, as Muslims, and sent to Turkey
questions.explain: The exchange sorted people by religion, so the Greek-speaking Vallahades were classified as Muslims and sent to Turkey.

qa.title: Who were the Vallahades?
answer: The Vallahades were Greek-speaking Muslims of western Macedonia, around Anaselitsa and Grevena. Their ancestors converted to Islam under Ottoman rule, but the community kept the Greek language and much of its Greek culture for generations.
In the population exchange between Greece and Turkey in 1923, people were sorted by religion, not language. The Vallahades were classified as Muslims and sent to Turkey.

quiz.title: How well do you know Bouboulina?
quiz.intro: Three quick questions from the film and its article.

questions.q: Which island was Laskarina Bouboulina from?
questions.explain: Bouboulina lived on Spetses, a shipowning island in the Saronic Gulf.

questions.q: What was the name of the warship she had built?
questions.explain: She commissioned and helped pay for the Agamemnon, armed with 18 cannons, and commanded it herself.

questions.q: Which Ottoman-held fortress did her ships blockade?
questions.explain: Her ships took part in the blockade of Nafplio, the most important fortress in the Peloponnese.

qa.title: Who was Laskarina Bouboulina?
answer: Laskarina Bouboulina was a shipowner from Spetses and a naval commander in the Greek War of Independence of 1821. After the deaths of her two husbands she managed their fortune and fleet herself.
She had the warship Agamemnon built and commanded it in the blockade of Nafplio. She was even arrested for a time by the revolutionary leadership, her own side, before being released.

quiz.title: How well do you know rebetiko?
quiz.intro: Three quick questions from the film and its article.

questions.q: Whose dictatorship formally censored rebetiko from 1936?
questions.explain: The Metaxas regime introduced censorship in 1936. Lyrics and recordings were reviewed and changed.

questions.q: Who brought much of rebetiko's sound to Piraeus and Athens?
questions.explain: Refugees from Smyrna, Constantinople and Asia Minor arrived with a musical world that shaped rebetiko.
The amané is an improvised, lamenting style of singing that came with the refugees from Asia Minor.

quiz.title: How well do you know the spoon sweet?
quiz.intro: Three quick questions about the film.

options: A cake baked for name days
Fruit preserved in thick syrup, served by the spoonful
A sweet wine from the islands
questions.explain: The spoon sweet is fruit preserved in syrup, offered to a guest on a small spoon.

questions.q: Why is it offered at a Greek door?
options: As a welcome to every guest
questions.explain: It was served to every guest who came to a Greek home, as a sign of welcome.

questions.q: The film's surprise: a spoonful of this sweet was once linked to...
options: A young woman's chances of marriage
questions.explain: As the film tells it, a Greek woman's chances of getting married once came down to a single spoonful of fruit.

qa.title: What is a Greek spoon sweet?
answer: A spoon sweet, glyko tou koutaliou in Greek, is fruit preserved in thick syrup. It is served on a small spoon, traditionally to every guest who arrives at a Greek home, as a gesture of hospitality.
Almost any fruit can be used: sour cherries, quince, figs, citrus peel, even young walnuts. For many families it is a taste of childhood, kept in a jar in the cupboard for visitors.

quiz.title: How well do you know the story of Tarpon Springs?
quiz.intro: Three quick questions from the film.

questions.q: Who organized the recruitment of Greek sponge divers to Tarpon Springs in 1905?
questions.explain: John Cocoris went back to Greece in 1905 and recruited sponge divers for Tarpon Springs, Florida.

questions.q: Which islands became famous for the sponge divers who followed?
questions.explain: The first recruits came from Aegina and Hydra. Then the great sponge-diving islands of the Dodecanese, Kalymnos, Symi and Halki, sent their own men.

questions.q: What is Tarpon Springs known for today?
options: The highest share of Greek-Americans of any city in the United States
The oldest Greek church in America
questions.explain: Tarpon Springs has the highest percentage of Greek-Americans of any city in the United States.

qa.title: Why are there so many Greeks in Tarpon Springs, Florida?
answer: In 1905 John Cocoris recruited Greek sponge divers to work the sponge beds off the Florida coast, bringing diving suits and methods the local industry had never used. Divers came first from Aegina and Hydra, then from the Dodecanese islands of Kalymnos, Symi and Halki.

The community built a church, a sponge exchange and a Greek town around the docks. Today Tarpon Springs has the highest percentage of Greek-Americans of any city in the United States, and its Epiphany cross dive is famous across the country.
